notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space.
  • Matter is composed of atoms, molecules or ions.
  • The common physical states of matter are solid, liquid and gas.
  • Plasma is an ionised state of matter.
  • Bose-Einstein condensate is a special state formed at extremely low temperatures.
  • Physical properties can be observed or measured without changing the chemical identity of a substance.
  • Density, elasticity, viscosity, surface tension and compressibility are important physical properties of matter.
  • Properties of matter depend on intermolecular forces and arrangement of particles.
  • Solids generally have the strongest intermolecular binding among the three common states.
  • Gases generally have much larger intermolecular separation than solids and liquids.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Matter → Mass + Occupies Space

2. Solid
  • Solids have definite shape and definite volume.
  • Particles in solids are closely packed.
  • Intermolecular forces are generally strong in solids.
  • Particles mainly vibrate about fixed equilibrium positions.
  • Solids are relatively incompressible.
  • Solids generally have high density compared with gases.
  • Solids can be crystalline or amorphous.
📌 Remember

Solid → Fixed Shape + Fixed Volume

3. Liquid
  • Liquids have definite volume but no definite shape.
  • A liquid takes the shape of its container.
  • Particles in liquids can move relative to one another.
  • Intermolecular forces in liquids are weaker than in most solids but stronger than in gases.
  • Liquids are only slightly compressible.
  • Liquids possess a free surface when placed in an open container.
  • Surface tension is an important property of liquids.
  • Liquids can flow and are therefore fluids.
📌 Remember

Liquid → Fixed Volume + No Fixed Shape

4. Gas
  • Gases have neither definite shape nor definite volume.
  • A gas expands to fill its container.
  • Gas particles are widely separated compared with solids and liquids.
  • Intermolecular forces are generally weak in gases under ordinary conditions.
  • Gases are highly compressible.
  • Gases exert pressure on the walls of their container.
  • Gases have much lower density than solids and liquids under ordinary conditions.
  • Gases are fluids.
📌 Remember

Gas → No Fixed Shape + No Fixed Volume

5. Plasma
  • Plasma is an ionised state of matter containing free electrons and ions.
  • Plasma conducts electricity.
  • Plasma responds strongly to electric and magnetic fields.
  • Stars, including the Sun, consist largely of plasma.
  • Lightning contains plasma.
  • Fluorescent lamps and neon signs contain ionised gases during operation.
  • Plasma is sometimes called the fourth state of matter.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Plasma → Ionised Gas → Free Charges

6. Bose-Einstein Condensate
  • Bose-Einstein condensate is abbreviated as BEC.
  • BEC forms when certain particles are cooled to temperatures very close to absolute zero.
  • In a BEC, many particles occupy the same quantum state.
  • Satyendra Nath Bose and Albert Einstein provided the theoretical basis for Bose-Einstein statistics.
  • The first dilute-gas Bose-Einstein condensates were experimentally produced in 1995.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

S. N. Bose + Einstein → Bose-Einstein Condensate

7. Intermolecular Force
  • Intermolecular forces act between molecules.
  • They influence melting point, boiling point, viscosity and surface tension.
  • Stronger intermolecular attraction generally makes particles harder to separate.
  • Intermolecular forces are not the same as chemical bonds within molecules.
  • Liquids exhibit both cohesion and adhesion because of intermolecular interactions.
8. Cohesion
  • Cohesion is the attractive force between molecules of the same substance.
  • Cohesion between water molecules contributes to surface tension.
  • Formation of droplets is influenced by cohesive forces.
  • Strong cohesion tends to make a liquid surface contract.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Cohesion → Same substance

9. Adhesion
  • Adhesion is attraction between molecules of different substances.
  • Water adhering to glass is an example of adhesion.
  • Adhesion plays an important role in capillary action.
  • The shape of a liquid meniscus depends on the balance between cohesive and adhesive forces.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Adhesion → Different substances

10. Cohesion vs Adhesion
  • Cohesion acts between similar molecules.
  • Adhesion acts between unlike molecules.
  • Water wets clean glass because adhesion between water and glass is stronger than water's cohesive effect at the boundary.
  • Mercury does not wet glass because cohesion within mercury is comparatively strong.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Cohesion → Same.

Adhesion → Different.

11. Density
  • Density is mass per unit volume.
  • Density is represented by ρ.
  • ρ = m/V.
  • SI unit of density is kg/m³.
  • Density is a scalar quantity.
  • Density of a substance can vary with temperature and pressure.
  • Solids and liquids are much less compressible than gases.
  • Gas density changes strongly with pressure and temperature.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Density → ρ = m/V → kg/m³

12. Density of Water
  • Pure water has maximum density at approximately 4°C.
  • The maximum density of water is approximately 1000 kg/m³.
  • This corresponds to approximately 1 g/cm³.
  • Water expands when cooled from 4°C toward 0°C.
  • This unusual behaviour is called anomalous expansion of water.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Water Maximum Density → 4°C

13. Anomalous Expansion of Water
  • Most substances contract on cooling.
  • Water contracts normally until approximately 4°C.
  • Below 4°C, water expands as it cools toward 0°C.
  • Ice is less dense than liquid water.
  • Ice therefore floats on water.
  • The anomalous behaviour of water helps lakes freeze from the surface downward.
  • Liquid water can remain beneath surface ice, helping aquatic life survive cold conditions.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Maximum density of water → 4°C, not 0°C.

14. Relative Density
  • Relative density is the ratio of the density of a substance to the density of a reference substance.
  • Water is usually the reference for solids and liquids.
  • Relative density is also called specific gravity in many contexts.
  • Relative density has no unit.
  • Relative density less than 1 indicates density lower than water when water is the reference.
  • Relative density greater than 1 indicates density greater than water.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Relative Density → No Unit

15. Specific Gravity
  • Specific gravity is another name commonly used for relative density.
  • It is dimensionless.
  • Specific gravity is a ratio and therefore has no SI unit.
  • A hydrometer can be used to measure specific gravity of liquids.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Density → Has unit.

Relative density / specific gravity → No unit.

16. Hydrometer
  • A hydrometer measures the relative density of liquids.
  • It works on the principle of floatation.
  • A hydrometer sinks deeper in a less dense liquid.
  • It floats higher in a denser liquid.
  • Hydrometers are calibrated for particular applications.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hydrometer → Relative Density → Floatation

17. Lactometer
  • A lactometer is a specialised hydrometer.
  • It is used to estimate the density or specific gravity of milk.
  • It can help detect dilution of milk with water, though density alone cannot determine complete milk quality.
  • It works on the principle of floatation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lactometer → Milk

18. Elasticity
  • Elasticity is the ability of a material to regain its original shape and size after removal of deforming force.
  • Elastic deformation is reversible.
  • A material can behave elastically only within a certain range of stress.
  • Elastic behaviour is related to intermolecular forces.
  • Steel is more elastic than rubber in the physics sense when elasticity is compared using Young's modulus.
  • Greater Young's modulus means greater resistance to deformation.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Steel is more elastic than rubber in terms of Young's modulus.

Rubber is more easily stretchable, but that does not mean it has a higher elastic modulus.

19. Plasticity
  • Plasticity is the ability of a material to undergo permanent deformation without breaking.
  • Plastic deformation remains after the deforming force is removed.
  • Clay shows high plasticity.
  • Metals can undergo plastic deformation during shaping.
  • Plasticity is useful in moulding and metalworking.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Elastic → Regains shape

Plastic → Permanent deformation

20. Deforming Force
  • A deforming force changes the size or shape of a body.
  • Deformation may involve stretching, compression, bending or twisting.
  • Internal restoring forces develop in an elastic material.
  • Removing the deforming force within the elastic limit allows recovery.
21. Stress
  • Stress is internal restoring force per unit area.
  • Stress = Force/Area.
  • SI unit of stress is pascal.
  • One pascal equals one newton per square metre.
  • Stress has the same SI unit as pressure.
  • Stress may be longitudinal, shear or bulk stress.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Stress → Force/Area → Pa

22. Strain
  • Strain is the fractional deformation produced by stress.
  • Longitudinal strain = Change in length / Original length.
  • Volume strain = Change in volume / Original volume.
  • Shear strain describes angular deformation.
  • Strain is dimensionless.
  • Strain has no unit.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Stress → Unit Pa.

Strain → No unit.

23. Hooke's Law
  • Hooke's Law applies within the proportional limit.
  • Stress is directly proportional to strain within the proportional limit.
  • For a spring, force is proportional to extension.
  • F = kx for an ideal spring within its elastic range.
  • Robert Hooke formulated the law.
  • Hooke's law fails beyond the proportional range.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hooke → Stress ∝ Strain

24. Elastic Limit
  • Elastic limit is the greatest stress up to which a material returns to its original shape after unloading.
  • Permanent deformation occurs when the elastic limit is exceeded.
  • The proportional limit and elastic limit are related but are not always exactly identical.
  • Hooke's law strictly applies within the proportional region.
25. Young's Modulus
  • Young's modulus measures resistance to longitudinal deformation.
  • Young's modulus = Longitudinal stress / Longitudinal strain.
  • It is represented by Y or E.
  • SI unit is pascal.
  • A larger Young's modulus indicates a stiffer material.
  • Steel has a much larger Young's modulus than rubber.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Young's Modulus → Longitudinal Stress / Longitudinal Strain

26. Bulk Modulus
  • Bulk modulus measures resistance to uniform compression.
  • Bulk modulus = Volume stress / Volume strain in magnitude.
  • It is represented by K.
  • SI unit is pascal.
  • A large bulk modulus indicates low compressibility.
  • Liquids have relatively high bulk modulus compared with gases.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bulk Modulus → Volume Change

27. Shear Modulus
  • Shear modulus measures resistance to change in shape under shear.
  • It is also called modulus of rigidity.
  • Shear modulus = Shear stress / Shear strain.
  • SI unit is pascal.
  • It is relevant to twisting and shear deformation of solids.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Shear Modulus → Rigidity

28. Compressibility
  • Compressibility measures how easily volume changes under pressure.
  • Compressibility is approximately the reciprocal of bulk modulus.
  • Gases have high compressibility.
  • Liquids have low compressibility.
  • Solids generally have very low compressibility.
  • High bulk modulus means low compressibility.
📌 Remember

Bulk Modulus ↑ → Compressibility ↓

29. Poisson's Ratio
  • When a material is stretched longitudinally, it generally contracts laterally.
  • Poisson's ratio relates lateral strain to longitudinal strain.
  • It is dimensionless.
  • Poisson's ratio has no unit.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Poisson's ratio → No unit.

30. Stress-Strain Curve
  • A stress-strain curve shows how a material responds to applied stress.
  • Initial linear behaviour follows Hooke's law for many materials.
  • The proportional limit marks the end of strict linearity.
  • Beyond the elastic region, permanent deformation may occur.
  • Ultimate tensile strength is the maximum stress a material can sustain before necking or failure depending on definition.
  • Fracture occurs when the material breaks.
31. Ductility
  • Ductility is the ability of a material to be drawn into wires.
  • Metals such as copper and gold are ductile.
  • Ductile materials undergo significant plastic deformation before fracture.
  • Copper's ductility makes it useful for electrical wiring.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ductility → Drawn into wires

32. Malleability
  • Malleability is the ability of a material to be hammered or rolled into sheets.
  • Gold is highly malleable.
  • Aluminium is malleable.
  • Malleability is an important property of many metals.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Malleability → Made into sheets

33. Ductility vs Malleability
  • Ductility refers to drawing into wires.
  • Malleability refers to forming sheets.
  • Gold is both highly ductile and highly malleable.
  • Copper is strongly ductile.
  • Aluminium is widely used in sheets and foils because of its malleability.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Ductility → Wire.

Malleability → Sheet.

34. Brittleness
  • A brittle material fractures with little plastic deformation.
  • Glass is brittle.
  • Ceramics are generally brittle.
  • Brittle materials may be strong under compression but weak under tensile or impact loading.
35. Hardness
  • Hardness is resistance to scratching, indentation or wear.
  • Diamond is one of the hardest naturally occurring materials.
  • Hardness is different from toughness.
  • A hard material may still be brittle.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Hardness ≠ Toughness.

36. Toughness
  • Toughness is the ability of a material to absorb energy before fracture.
  • Tough materials resist crack propagation and impact damage.
  • Toughness depends on both strength and ability to deform.
  • A brittle material generally has low toughness.
37. Strength
  • Strength is the ability of a material to withstand applied stress without failure.
  • Tensile strength concerns pulling forces.
  • Compressive strength concerns squeezing forces.
  • Shear strength concerns sliding forces.
  • Different materials may be strong under one type of loading and weaker under another.
38. Crystalline Solid
  • Crystalline solids have long-range ordered arrangement of particles.
  • Crystals have a regular repeating structure.
  • Crystalline solids generally have definite melting points.
  • Sodium chloride is a crystalline solid.
  • Quartz is crystalline.
  • Most metals are crystalline on microscopic scales.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Crystalline → Long-range order + Definite melting point

39. Amorphous Solid
  • Amorphous solids lack long-range crystalline order.
  • Glass is a common amorphous solid.
  • Amorphous solids soften over a range of temperatures rather than melting sharply.
  • Rubber and many plastics can have amorphous regions.
  • Amorphous solids are generally isotropic on large scales.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Amorphous → No long-range order

40. Crystalline vs Amorphous
  • Crystalline solids have ordered internal structure.
  • Amorphous solids lack long-range order.
  • Crystalline solids generally have sharper melting points.
  • Amorphous solids soften gradually over a range.
  • Crystals may show anisotropy.
  • Amorphous solids are generally isotropic.
41. Isotropy
  • An isotropic material has the same physical properties in all directions.
  • Gases and liquids are generally isotropic at macroscopic scales.
  • Amorphous solids are generally isotropic.
  • Isotropy means direction-independent properties.
42. Anisotropy
  • An anisotropic material has physical properties that vary with direction.
  • Many crystals are anisotropic.
  • Electrical, optical or mechanical properties may depend on direction within a crystal.
  • Anisotropy arises from directional internal structure.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Isotropic → Same in all directions

Anisotropic → Direction-dependent

43. Surface Tension
  • Surface tension is the tendency of a liquid surface to minimise its area.
  • It arises mainly from cohesive intermolecular forces.
  • Molecules inside a liquid experience approximately balanced attractions.
  • Surface molecules experience a net inward cohesive effect.
  • Surface tension makes a liquid surface behave somewhat like a stretched membrane.
  • SI unit of surface tension is N/m.
  • Surface tension can also be interpreted as surface energy per unit area.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Surface Tension → Cohesion → Minimum Surface Area

44. Unit of Surface Tension
  • SI unit of surface tension is newton per metre.
  • N/m is equivalent dimensionally to joule per square metre for surface energy.
  • Surface tension is commonly represented by γ or T.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Surface tension → N/m.

Not N/m².

45. Surface Tension and Temperature
  • Surface tension of a liquid generally decreases as temperature increases.
  • At the critical temperature, distinction between liquid and gas disappears and surface tension approaches zero.
  • Heating weakens the effective cohesive behaviour of the surface.
📌 Remember

Temperature ↑ → Surface Tension generally ↓

46. Effect of Detergent
  • Soap and detergents reduce the surface tension of water.
  • Lower surface tension improves wetting.
  • Better wetting helps water penetrate fabrics and remove dirt.
  • Detergents act as surfactants.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Soap/Detergent → Surface Tension ↓ → Wetting ↑

47. Surfactant
  • A surfactant reduces surface tension at an interface.
  • Soap and detergents are surfactants.
  • Surfactants help emulsify grease and oil.
  • Surfactants are widely used in cleaning, medicine and industry.
48. Surface Area of a Sphere
  • For a given volume, a sphere has the minimum surface area.
  • Surface tension therefore tends to make small free liquid drops approximately spherical.
  • Very small droplets appear more spherical than large drops strongly affected by gravity.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Surface Tension → Drops become spherical

49. Water Droplets
  • Small water droplets tend to be spherical because surface tension minimises surface area.
  • Gravity distorts larger droplets.
  • Raindrops are not perfectly tear-shaped while freely falling.
  • Small raindrops are nearly spherical.
50. Soap Bubble
  • A soap bubble has two liquid-air surfaces.
  • Excess pressure inside a soap bubble is greater than in a single liquid drop of the same radius and surface tension.
  • For a soap bubble, excess pressure ΔP = 4T/r.
  • For a liquid drop with one surface, ΔP = 2T/r.
  • Smaller bubbles have greater excess internal pressure.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Liquid Drop → 2T/r

Soap Bubble → 4T/r

51. Angle of Contact
  • Angle of contact is the angle between the tangent to the liquid surface and the solid surface at the point of contact, measured through the liquid.
  • The angle depends on the liquid-solid pair.
  • Water on clean glass has an acute contact angle.
  • Mercury on glass has an obtuse contact angle.
  • Contact angle helps determine whether a liquid wets a surface.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Water + Glass → Acute angle

Mercury + Glass → Obtuse angle

52. Wetting
  • A liquid wets a surface when adhesive forces between liquid and surface dominate sufficiently over cohesive effects.
  • Water wets clean glass.
  • Mercury does not wet glass.
  • Detergents improve wetting by lowering water's surface tension.
53. Meniscus
  • A meniscus is the curved surface of a liquid in a narrow container.
  • Water forms a concave meniscus in clean glass.
  • Mercury forms a convex meniscus in glass.
  • Meniscus shape depends on adhesion and cohesion.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Water in glass → Concave.

Mercury in glass → Convex.

54. Capillarity
  • Capillarity is the rise or fall of a liquid in a narrow tube.
  • It results from surface tension together with adhesive and cohesive forces.
  • Water rises in a narrow glass capillary.
  • Mercury is depressed in a glass capillary.
  • Narrower capillary tubes generally produce greater capillary rise for a wetting liquid.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Capillary radius ↓ → Rise ↑

55. Capillary Rise Formula
  • For a narrow circular tube, capillary rise is approximately h = 2T cosθ / ρgr.
  • h is capillary height.
  • T is surface tension.
  • θ is angle of contact.
  • ρ is liquid density.
  • r is tube radius.
  • Capillary rise is inversely proportional to tube radius.
56. Applications of Capillarity
  • Kerosene rises through a lamp wick by capillary action.
  • Ink can move through fine pores by capillarity.
  • Water moves through small pores in soil partly because of capillary forces.
  • Towels absorb water through capillary action in fine spaces.
  • Blotting paper absorbs liquids by capillarity.
  • Plant water transport involves several processes, including capillary effects, cohesion-tension and transpiration.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Capillarity contributes to plant water movement, but it is not the sole mechanism responsible for ascent of sap in tall plants.

57. Viscosity
  • Viscosity is resistance to relative motion between adjacent layers of a fluid.
  • It is often described as internal friction of a fluid.
  • Honey has greater viscosity than water at room temperature.
  • Greater viscosity means greater resistance to flow.
  • Viscosity affects flow through pipes and around moving objects.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Viscosity → Internal Fluid Friction

58. Dynamic Viscosity
  • Dynamic viscosity is commonly represented by η.
  • SI unit of dynamic viscosity is pascal-second.
  • Pa·s is equivalent to N s/m².
  • Poise is a CGS unit of dynamic viscosity.
  • One poise equals 0.1 Pa·s.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Viscosity SI Unit → Pa·s

59. Viscosity and Temperature
  • Viscosity of liquids generally decreases with rise in temperature.
  • Heating gives liquid molecules greater mobility.
  • Viscosity of gases generally increases with temperature.
  • The temperature dependence of gas viscosity differs from that of liquids.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Liquids → Temperature ↑, Viscosity ↓

Gases → Temperature ↑, Viscosity ↑

60. Stokes' Law
  • Stokes' Law gives the viscous drag on a small sphere moving slowly through a viscous fluid.
  • The drag force is F = 6πηrv.
  • η is viscosity.
  • r is radius of the sphere.
  • v is speed relative to the fluid.
  • George Gabriel Stokes is associated with this law.
  • Stokes' Law applies under low-Reynolds-number laminar-flow conditions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Stokes → Viscous Drag → 6πηrv

61. Terminal Velocity
  • A falling body in a fluid may eventually reach terminal velocity.
  • At terminal velocity, net force is zero.
  • Weight is balanced by buoyancy and drag.
  • Acceleration becomes zero.
  • The object then falls with constant velocity.
  • Increasing drag reduces terminal velocity.
  • Parachutes reduce terminal velocity by increasing drag.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Terminal Velocity → Net Force 0 → Constant Velocity

62. Laminar Flow
  • Laminar flow is smooth fluid motion in which layers move with little mixing.
  • Streamlines do not cross in ideal laminar flow.
  • Laminar flow commonly occurs at low speeds and high viscosity.
  • Viscous forces dominate in low-Reynolds-number flow.
63. Turbulent Flow
  • Turbulent flow involves irregular eddies and mixing.
  • Turbulence is more likely at high flow speeds.
  • Turbulence generally increases resistance to flow.
  • Reynolds number helps indicate whether flow is likely to be laminar or turbulent.
64. Reynolds Number
  • Reynolds number is a dimensionless quantity used in fluid mechanics.
  • It compares inertial effects with viscous effects.
  • Low Reynolds number favours laminar flow.
  • High Reynolds number favours turbulent flow.
  • Reynolds number has no unit.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Reynolds Number → Laminar vs Turbulent Flow

65. Diffusion
  • Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration due to random molecular motion.
  • Diffusion occurs in gases, liquids and solids.
  • Diffusion is fastest in gases among the common states under comparable conditions.
  • Diffusion is slower in liquids than in gases.
  • Diffusion in solids is generally very slow.
  • Temperature increase generally increases diffusion rate.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Diffusion → High Concentration → Low Concentration

66. Examples of Diffusion
  • Perfume spreading through a room is diffusion in air.
  • Ink spreading through water demonstrates diffusion in a liquid.
  • Gas exchange in lungs involves diffusion.
  • Oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse across respiratory surfaces.
  • Nutrient and waste movement across biological membranes may involve diffusion.
67. Osmosis
  • Osmosis is the net movement of solvent molecules through a selectively permeable membrane.
  • Solvent moves from a region of higher solvent potential or lower solute concentration toward lower solvent potential or higher solute concentration under standard descriptions.
  • Water is the solvent in most biological osmosis examples.
  • Osmosis is important in plant and animal cells.
  • Osmosis differs from ordinary diffusion because a selectively permeable membrane is essential.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Osmosis → Solvent + Selectively Permeable Membrane

68. Diffusion vs Osmosis
  • Diffusion can involve solute or gas particles.
  • Osmosis specifically refers to movement of solvent through a selectively permeable membrane.
  • Diffusion does not always require a membrane.
  • Osmosis requires a selectively permeable membrane.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Every osmosis process involves solvent movement.

Not every diffusion process is osmosis.

69. Brownian Motion
  • Brownian motion is the random motion of microscopic particles suspended in a fluid.
  • It results from uneven collisions with surrounding molecules.
  • Robert Brown observed this phenomenon in pollen particles suspended in water in 1827.
  • Brownian motion provided important evidence for molecular motion.
  • Albert Einstein gave a theoretical explanation of Brownian motion in 1905.
  • Jean Perrin experimentally studied Brownian motion and helped confirm atomic theory.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Robert Brown → Brownian Motion → 1827

70. Kinetic Theory of Matter
  • Kinetic theory explains matter in terms of constantly moving particles.
  • Particles in matter possess kinetic energy.
  • Particle motion generally increases as temperature increases.
  • In gases, particles move randomly in all directions.
  • Gas pressure results from collisions of molecules with container walls.
  • Intermolecular separation is much greater in gases than in liquids or solids.
71. Gas Pressure
  • Gas pressure results from molecular collisions with container walls.
  • Increasing gas temperature at constant volume generally increases pressure.
  • Increasing gas volume at constant temperature generally decreases pressure.
  • Gas pressure acts in all directions in a stationary container.
72. Compressibility of Matter
  • Gases are highly compressible because there is large empty space between particles.
  • Liquids are only slightly compressible.
  • Solids are very difficult to compress.
  • Compressibility is important in gas storage.
  • Compressed gases are stored under high pressure in suitable cylinders.
73. Fluid
  • A fluid is a substance that can flow.
  • Liquids are fluids.
  • Gases are fluids.
  • Fluids cannot sustain a static shear stress indefinitely.
  • Fluid mechanics includes hydrostatics and hydrodynamics.
74. Hydrostatics
  • Hydrostatics deals with fluids at rest.
  • Pressure in a static liquid increases with depth.
  • Pascal's principle is an important hydrostatic principle.
  • Archimedes' principle is important in hydrostatics.
75. Hydrodynamics
  • Hydrodynamics deals with liquids in motion.
  • Fluid speed, pressure and flow rate are important hydrodynamic quantities.
  • Bernoulli's principle relates pressure and speed under suitable flow conditions.
  • The continuity equation represents conservation of mass in fluid flow.
76. Pressure
  • Pressure is force per unit area.
  • P = F/A.
  • SI unit is pascal.
  • One pascal equals one newton per square metre.
  • Smaller area produces greater pressure for the same force.
  • Pressure is a scalar quantity.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pressure → F/A → Pa

77. Atmospheric Pressure
  • Atmospheric pressure is caused by the weight and molecular motion of the atmosphere.
  • Atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude.
  • Standard atmospheric pressure at sea level is approximately 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa.
  • One atmosphere is approximately 101.3 kPa.
  • Atmospheric pressure is commonly measured using a barometer.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Atmospheric Pressure → Barometer

78. Torricelli and Barometer
  • Evangelista Torricelli invented the mercury barometer.
  • The traditional mercury barometer uses a mercury column.
  • Standard atmospheric pressure supports approximately 760 mm of mercury.
  • 760 mm Hg is approximately one atmosphere.
  • Torricelli demonstrated that the atmosphere exerts pressure.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Torricelli → Mercury Barometer

79. Barometer
  • A barometer measures atmospheric pressure.
  • Mercury barometers use a mercury column.
  • Aneroid barometers do not use liquid.
  • Falling atmospheric pressure can be associated with approaching low-pressure weather systems.
  • Rising atmospheric pressure can be associated with relatively stable high-pressure conditions.
80. Manometer
  • A manometer measures pressure or pressure difference of gases and liquids.
  • A U-tube manometer is a common form.
  • Pressure difference causes different liquid levels in the arms.
  • Manometers are commonly used in laboratories and industry.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Barometer → Atmospheric pressure.

Manometer → Pressure of confined fluid / pressure difference.

81. Pascal's Principle
  • Pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout the fluid under ideal conditions.
  • Hydraulic brakes use Pascal's principle.
  • Hydraulic lifts use Pascal's principle.
  • Hydraulic presses use Pascal's principle.
  • Blaise Pascal is associated with the law.
82. Archimedes' Principle
  • A body immersed wholly or partly in a fluid experiences an upward buoyant force.
  • Buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced fluid.
  • Archimedes' principle applies to both liquids and gases.
  • It explains apparent loss of weight in a fluid.
  • It is used in designing ships and submarines.
83. Buoyancy
  • Buoyancy is the upward force exerted by a fluid.
  • Buoyancy arises because pressure is greater at greater depth.
  • An object floats when buoyant force balances its weight.
  • An object sinks when its weight exceeds the maximum available buoyant force for its condition.
  • Hot-air balloons rise because the average density of the balloon system can become less than surrounding air.
84. Law of Floatation
  • A floating body displaces a weight of fluid equal to its own weight.
  • A ship floats because its overall average density is less than that of water.
  • A submarine controls buoyancy using ballast tanks.
  • Ice floats because ice is less dense than liquid water.
85. Surface Energy
  • Molecules at the liquid surface possess greater potential energy than molecules deep inside the liquid.
  • Increasing surface area requires work.
  • Surface energy is related to surface tension.
  • Liquids tend to minimise surface area when no external forces dominate.
86. Evaporation and Surface Area
  • Evaporation occurs at the surface of a liquid.
  • Greater surface area generally increases evaporation rate.
  • Higher temperature generally increases evaporation rate.
  • Increased airflow generally increases evaporation rate.
  • Higher humidity generally reduces evaporation rate.
  • Evaporation produces cooling because higher-energy molecules preferentially escape.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Evaporation → Surface phenomenon + Cooling

87. Evaporation vs Boiling
  • Evaporation can occur at any temperature below the boiling point.
  • Evaporation occurs mainly at the surface.
  • Boiling occurs throughout the liquid when vapour pressure equals external pressure.
  • Boiling occurs at a characteristic temperature for a given pressure.
  • Evaporation is generally slower than boiling.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Evaporation → Surface + Any temperature.

Boiling → Throughout liquid + Boiling point.

88. Melting
  • Melting is the conversion of solid into liquid.
  • Melting occurs when particles gain sufficient energy to overcome part of the solid structure.
  • A pure crystalline substance has a characteristic melting point at a specified pressure.
  • Amorphous solids generally soften over a range of temperatures.
89. Freezing
  • Freezing is the conversion of liquid into solid.
  • For a pure substance at a given pressure, freezing point and melting point are the same equilibrium temperature.
  • Freezing involves increased ordering of particles in crystalline substances.
90. Vaporisation
  • Vaporisation is conversion of liquid into gas.
  • Evaporation and boiling are two forms of vaporisation.
  • Evaporation occurs at the surface.
  • Boiling occurs throughout the liquid.
91. Condensation
  • Condensation is conversion of gas or vapour into liquid.
  • Cooling commonly causes condensation.
  • Water droplets on a cold surface form by condensation of water vapour.
  • Clouds form when water vapour condenses on tiny particles under suitable atmospheric conditions.
92. Sublimation
  • Sublimation is direct conversion of a solid into gas without passing through the liquid state under suitable conditions.
  • Camphor undergoes sublimation.
  • Naphthalene can sublime.
  • Iodine can sublime upon heating.
  • Dry ice changes directly from solid carbon dioxide to gas at ordinary atmospheric pressure.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Camphor + Naphthalene + Iodine + Dry Ice → Sublimation

93. Deposition
  • Deposition is direct conversion of gas into solid.
  • Deposition is the reverse of sublimation.
  • Frost formation can involve deposition of water vapour directly as ice.
  • Deposition is also called desublimation.
94. Triple Point
  • The triple point is the unique temperature and pressure at which solid, liquid and gas phases coexist in equilibrium.
  • The triple point is characteristic of a pure substance.
  • Water's triple point historically played an important role in temperature standards.
95. Critical Point
  • The critical point is the end of the liquid-gas phase boundary.
  • Above the critical temperature, a gas cannot be liquefied by pressure alone.
  • Above the critical point, liquid and gas phases become indistinguishable as a supercritical fluid.
  • Surface tension approaches zero near the critical point.
96. Crystalline Melting
  • Crystalline solids generally possess a definite melting point.
  • Their particles are arranged in regular repeating structures.
  • Melting disrupts the ordered crystal lattice.
  • Impurities often lower and broaden the melting range.
97. Thermal Expansion — Basic Fact
  • Most materials expand when heated.
  • Thermal expansion occurs because average particle separation increases.
  • Solids show linear, area and volume expansion.
  • Liquids primarily exhibit volume expansion.
  • Gases expand strongly when heated under suitable conditions.
  • Water shows anomalous behaviour between 0°C and 4°C.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Most substances expand on heating.

Water between 0°C and 4°C is an important exception to ordinary behaviour.

98. Linear Expansion
  • Linear expansion refers to change in length with temperature.
  • ΔL = αL₀ΔT.
  • α is coefficient of linear expansion.
  • α generally depends on the material.
  • Expansion joints are provided in bridges and railway tracks to accommodate thermal expansion.
99. Bimetallic Strip
  • A bimetallic strip consists of two different metals bonded together.
  • The metals have different coefficients of thermal expansion.
  • Heating causes the strip to bend.
  • Bimetallic strips are used in thermostats.
  • They are also used in some circuit breakers and thermal switches.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bimetallic Strip → Different Expansion → Thermostat

100. Brownian Motion and Evidence for Molecules
  • Brownian motion demonstrates continuous molecular activity.
  • Random collisions of fluid molecules cause suspended particles to move irregularly.
  • The movement becomes more vigorous at higher temperature.
  • Brownian motion was important historical evidence supporting atomic and molecular theory.
101. Important Scientist–Concept Pairs
  • Robert Hooke → Elasticity / Hooke's Law.
  • Thomas Young → Young's modulus named after him.
  • Blaise Pascal → Fluid pressure.
  • Archimedes → Buoyancy.
  • Evangelista Torricelli → Barometer.
  • George Gabriel Stokes → Viscous drag.
  • Robert Brown → Brownian motion.
  • Satyendra Nath Bose → Bose-Einstein statistics.
  • Albert Einstein → Brownian-motion theory and Bose-Einstein work.
  • Daniel Bernoulli → Fluid-flow principle.
102. Important Formulae
  • Density → ρ = m/V.
  • Pressure → P = F/A.
  • Hydrostatic pressure → P = ρgh.
  • Stress → F/A.
  • Longitudinal strain → ΔL/L.
  • Young's modulus → Longitudinal stress / Longitudinal strain.
  • Bulk modulus → Volume stress / Volume strain.
  • Shear modulus → Shear stress / Shear strain.
  • Hooke's spring law → F = kx.
  • Capillary rise → h = 2T cosθ / ρgr.
  • Liquid drop excess pressure → 2T/r.
  • Soap bubble excess pressure → 4T/r.
  • Stokes drag → F = 6πηrv.
  • Linear thermal expansion → ΔL = αL₀ΔT.
103. Important SI Units
  • Density → kg/m³.
  • Pressure → pascal.
  • Stress → pascal.
  • Young's modulus → pascal.
  • Bulk modulus → pascal.
  • Shear modulus → pascal.
  • Surface tension → N/m.
  • Dynamic viscosity → Pa·s.
  • Force → newton.
  • Volume → m³.
  • Relative density → No unit.
  • Strain → No unit.
  • Poisson's ratio → No unit.
  • Reynolds number → No unit.
104. Must-Memorise Matter Properties
  • Density → Mass/Volume.
  • Relative density → Density ratio.
  • Elasticity → Regains shape.
  • Plasticity → Permanent deformation.
  • Ductility → Wire.
  • Malleability → Sheet.
  • Hardness → Resistance to scratching/indentation.
  • Toughness → Energy before fracture.
  • Viscosity → Resistance to flow.
  • Surface tension → Surface minimises area.
  • Cohesion → Same molecules.
  • Adhesion → Different molecules.
  • Capillarity → Rise/fall in narrow tube.
  • Diffusion → High to low concentration.
  • Osmosis → Solvent through selective membrane.
  • Brownian motion → Random suspended-particle motion.
105. Must-Memorise Instruments
  • Hydrometer → Relative density of liquids.
  • Lactometer → Milk density.
  • Barometer → Atmospheric pressure.
  • Manometer → Fluid pressure / pressure difference.
  • Thermostat → Often uses bimetallic strip.
  • Viscometer → Measures viscosity.
106. TNPSC Traps
  • Matter has mass and occupies space.
  • Plasma is an ionised state of matter.
  • BEC forms near absolute zero.
  • Relative density has no unit.
  • Density has unit kg/m³.
  • Water has maximum density at about 4°C.
  • Ice is less dense than water.
  • Steel is more elastic than rubber in terms of elastic modulus.
  • Elasticity and stretchability are not the same.
  • Stress has unit pascal.
  • Strain has no unit.
  • Young's modulus has unit pascal.
  • Bulk modulus is inversely related to compressibility.
  • Ductility means wire; malleability means sheet.
  • Crystalline solids have long-range order.
  • Glass is amorphous.
  • Surface tension decreases with temperature.
  • Detergents reduce water's surface tension.
  • Surface tension unit is N/m, not N/m².
  • Water forms concave meniscus in glass.
  • Mercury forms convex meniscus in glass.
  • Water rises in glass capillary.
  • Mercury is depressed in glass capillary.
  • Narrower capillary gives greater rise.
  • Viscosity of liquids generally decreases on heating.
  • Viscosity of gases generally increases on heating.
  • Terminal velocity occurs when net force becomes zero.
  • Brownian motion is caused by molecular collisions.
  • Diffusion does not require a membrane.
  • Osmosis requires a selectively permeable membrane.
  • Gas is more compressible than liquid or solid.
  • Barometer measures atmospheric pressure.
  • Manometer measures pressure difference or confined-fluid pressure.
  • Sublimation bypasses the liquid state.
  • Deposition is gas directly to solid.
  • Evaporation can occur below boiling point.
  • Evaporation is a surface process.
  • Boiling occurs throughout the liquid.
  • Water's anomalous expansion occurs between 0°C and 4°C.
107. Ultra-Short Memory Chain
  • Matter → Mass + Space.
  • Solid → Shape + Volume fixed.
  • Liquid → Volume fixed.
  • Gas → Neither fixed.
  • Plasma → Ionised.
  • BEC → Near absolute zero.
  • Density → m/V.
  • Water max density → 4°C.
  • Relative density → No unit.
  • Hydrometer → Liquid density.
  • Lactometer → Milk.
  • Elasticity → Recover.
  • Plasticity → Permanent.
  • Stress → F/A.
  • Strain → No unit.
  • Young → Longitudinal.
  • Bulk → Volume.
  • Shear → Shape.
  • Ductility → Wire.
  • Malleability → Sheet.
  • Surface tension → N/m.
  • Detergent → Surface tension ↓.
  • Water meniscus → Concave.
  • Mercury meniscus → Convex.
  • Capillarity → Narrow tube.
  • Viscosity → Internal friction.
  • Stokes → 6πηrv.
  • Brown → Brownian motion.
  • Diffusion → High to low.
  • Osmosis → Solvent + membrane.
  • Barometer → Atmospheric pressure.
  • Pascal → Hydraulic pressure.
  • Archimedes → Buoyancy.
  • Sublimation → Solid to gas.
  • Deposition → Gas to solid.
Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected
  • Matter means? → Anything having mass and occupying space.
  • Three common states of matter? → Solid, liquid and gas.
  • Fourth state of matter commonly called? → Plasma.
  • Plasma consists mainly of? → Ions and free electrons.
  • State formed near absolute zero? → Bose-Einstein condensate.
  • Indian scientist associated with BEC theory? → Satyendra Nath Bose.
  • Solid has? → Definite shape and volume.
  • Liquid has? → Definite volume but no definite shape.
  • Gas has? → Neither definite shape nor definite volume.
  • Attraction between same molecules? → Cohesion.
  • Attraction between different substances? → Adhesion.
  • Density formula? → ρ = m/V.
  • SI unit of density? → kg/m³.
  • Maximum density of water occurs at? → About 4°C.
  • Approximate maximum density of water? → 1000 kg/m³.
  • Why does ice float? → Ice is less dense than liquid water.
  • Unusual expansion of water below 4°C? → Anomalous expansion.
  • Relative density has unit? → No.
  • Another name for relative density? → Specific gravity.
  • Instrument measuring relative density of liquid? → Hydrometer.
  • Instrument used for milk density? → Lactometer.
  • Ability to regain original shape? → Elasticity.
  • Permanent-deformation property? → Plasticity.
  • Which is more elastic in physics terms, steel or rubber? → Steel.
  • Stress formula? → Force/Area.
  • SI unit of stress? → Pascal.
  • Strain unit? → No unit.
  • Hooke's Law? → Stress is proportional to strain within proportional limit.
  • Scientist associated with Hooke's Law? → Robert Hooke.
  • Young's modulus measures? → Resistance to longitudinal deformation.
  • Bulk modulus measures? → Resistance to volume compression.
  • Shear modulus is also called? → Modulus of rigidity.
  • Compressibility is approximately reciprocal of? → Bulk modulus.
  • Poisson's ratio unit? → No unit.
  • Ability to draw material into wire? → Ductility.
  • Ability to make material into sheets? → Malleability.
  • Highly malleable metal? → Gold.
  • Material with long-range ordered structure? → Crystalline solid.
  • Common amorphous solid? → Glass.
  • Crystalline solids generally show? → Definite melting point.
  • Amorphous solids generally? → Soften over a temperature range.
  • Same properties in all directions? → Isotropic.
  • Direction-dependent properties? → Anisotropic.
  • Property causing liquid surface to minimise area? → Surface tension.
  • Cause of surface tension? → Cohesive molecular forces.
  • SI unit of surface tension? → N/m.
  • Effect of temperature rise on liquid surface tension? → Generally decreases.
  • Effect of detergent on water surface tension? → Decreases it.
  • Why are small liquid drops spherical? → Surface tension minimises surface area.
  • Excess pressure in liquid drop? → 2T/r.
  • Excess pressure in soap bubble? → 4T/r.
  • Water meniscus in glass? → Concave.
  • Mercury meniscus in glass? → Convex.
  • Water-glass contact angle? → Acute.
  • Mercury-glass contact angle? → Obtuse.
  • Rise or fall of liquid in narrow tube? → Capillarity.
  • Water in clean glass capillary? → Rises.
  • Mercury in glass capillary? → Falls/depresses.
  • Capillary rise is inversely proportional to? → Tube radius.
  • Lamp wick works mainly through? → Capillary action.
  • Blotting paper absorbs liquid by? → Capillarity.
  • Internal friction of a fluid? → Viscosity.
  • SI unit of dynamic viscosity? → Pa·s.
  • Viscosity of liquid on heating? → Generally decreases.
  • Viscosity of gas on heating? → Generally increases.
  • Viscous drag on small sphere described by? → Stokes' Law.
  • Stokes' Law formula? → F = 6πηrv.
  • Scientist associated with Stokes' Law? → George Gabriel Stokes.
  • Constant falling speed in fluid after forces balance? → Terminal velocity.
  • At terminal velocity, acceleration? → Zero.
  • Smooth layered fluid flow? → Laminar flow.
  • Irregular eddying flow? → Turbulent flow.
  • Dimensionless quantity distinguishing laminar and turbulent flow? → Reynolds number.
  • Net movement from higher to lower concentration? → Diffusion.
  • In which common state is diffusion fastest? → Gas.
  • Movement of solvent through selectively permeable membrane? → Osmosis.
  • Does diffusion always require a membrane? → No.
  • Does osmosis require a selectively permeable membrane? → Yes.
  • Random motion of suspended microscopic particles? → Brownian motion.
  • Brownian motion observed by? → Robert Brown.
  • Year associated with Robert Brown's observation? → 1827.
  • Brownian motion theoretical explanation associated with? → Albert Einstein.
  • Gas pressure results mainly from? → Molecular collisions with container walls.
  • Most compressible common state? → Gas.
  • Branch dealing with fluids at rest? → Hydrostatics.
  • Branch dealing with moving liquids? → Hydrodynamics.
  • Pressure formula? → P = F/A.
  • SI unit of pressure? → Pascal.
  • Standard atmospheric pressure approximately? → 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa.
  • Equivalent standard mercury column? → About 760 mm Hg.
  • Instrument measuring atmospheric pressure? → Barometer.
  • Mercury barometer invented by? → Evangelista Torricelli.
  • Instrument measuring pressure difference? → Manometer.
  • Hydraulic machines work on? → Pascal's principle.
  • Upward fluid force? → Buoyant force.
  • Archimedes' Principle? → Buoyant force equals weight of displaced fluid.
  • Floating body displaces fluid of weight equal to? → Its own weight.
  • Direct solid-to-gas change? → Sublimation.
  • Examples of sublimating substances? → Camphor, naphthalene, iodine and dry ice.
  • Direct gas-to-solid change? → Deposition.
  • Liquid-to-gas conversion at surface below boiling point? → Evaporation.
  • Does evaporation cause cooling? → Yes.
  • Boiling occurs where? → Throughout the liquid.
  • Unique point where solid, liquid and gas coexist? → Triple point.
  • Point beyond which liquid and gas become indistinguishable? → Critical point.
  • Most substances on heating? → Expand.
  • Device using different thermal expansion of two metals? → Bimetallic strip.
  • Bimetallic strip commonly used in? → Thermostats.
  • Core TNPSC memory line? → Density, Elasticity, Surface Tension, Viscosity, Capillarity, Pressure and Buoyancy are the major high-yield properties of matter.
